podcast.title: Accidental "Perfect" Take
podcast.body: While engineering a session for Trevor Horn with session pianist Nick Piotis on a Steinway Grand, Chris Berkett was tweaking the EQ during the take, not intending to record the final version. Trevor Horn declared it "the take," forcing Berkett to meticulously reverse his real-time EQ changes to save the performance, which taught him not to interfere with the performance itself. "I said, well, we can't use that. I was changing all the EQ. I was filling with the sound while it was... And he goes, well, that's your problem. We're going out for dinner. You fix it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Capturing Performance Over Technical Perfection
podcast.body: Chris Berkett prioritizes capturing a spontaneous, authentic performance over meticulous technical adjustments. He uses a single, trusted microphone (AKG 414 B-ULS) and avoids excessive tweaking during recording sessions to ensure artists aren't exhausted and crucial moments aren't missed. "I want to capture performance, like, like nothing compares to you, and she probably knows she needs song, that was a one take vocal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Daughter's Singing Opportunity with Bob Geldof
podcast.body: Chris Berkett's then 16-year-old daughter had the opportunity to sing on one of Bob Geldof's records. "My 16-year-old daughter at the time sang on one of his records, which is a great opportunity for her."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Designing and Building Tapestry Studios
podcast.body: After leaving Omaha Sheriff and working as a milkman, Chris Berkett was asked by John Kongos to design and build his new studio in London, Tapestry Studios, leveraging his electronics degree. "Would you like to come and design and build my new studio?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career Mentorship with Tony Visconti
podcast.body: Chris Berkett signed a deal for a couple of albums with Tony Visconti and his band Omaha Sheriff. While in the studio, Berkett constantly asked Visconti questions due to his electronics degree, learning how to make records by observing him. "I learned how to make records by watching Tony."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Engineer's Role as Unsung Hero
podcast.body: Chris Berkett regards engineers as "unsung heroes" responsible for the technical aspects of recording, from capturing source sounds to mixing and balancing. He was a "creative musical engineer" and highly sought after in London during the 1980s. "An engineer. They're the kind of... The unsung heroes of music, in my opinion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Recording Experience with Tape Handling Error
podcast.body: As an engineer at Tapestry Studios, Chris Berkett's first recording session involved a big horn section (possibly for "Geno" by Dexys Midnight Runners). He mistakenly put the 24-track, two-inch tape on backward, resulting in a "wooly" sound, learning from the error without prior instruction. "I realized I put the tape on back to front. No, nobody told me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Multi-Instrumentalist Producer
podcast.body: Chris Berkett became a multi-instrumentalist (piano, bass, drums, guitar) to effectively communicate with musicians in the studio, often by demonstrating desired grooves or parts directly on the instrument rather than solely relying on written scores or verbal explanations. "I had to learn piano, bass, drums, and play, and then to play everything so that I could communicate with the musicians that are making the records in the right way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Patience in the Studio
podcast.body: As a producer, Chris Berkett emphasizes the need for enormous patience, citing an experience with the Buena Vista Social Club trumpet player where 250 takes were recorded for a solo, requiring extensive editing. "You have to sit there sometimes for hours."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering African Samples with "Afro-Dizzy Act"
podcast.body: Chris Berkett wrote "Afro-Dizzy Act," which became a huge club hit in England and was notable as the first song to use African samples, well before others adopted the technique. "that's the first song to use, African samples. It's way before anybody else did it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Preference for Melodyne for Vocal Tuning
podcast.body: Chris Berkett prefers Melodyne over Auto-Tune for vocal tuning due to its transparency. He uses it sparingly to correct only specific, irritating notes in an otherwise good performance, leaving the majority of the vocal natural, as he did with Buffy St. Marie. "I use a program called Melodyne, which is the most transparent tuning program I've ever discovered."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Producer's Role as Liaison
podcast.body: Chris Berkett defines a music producer's role as a liaison between the artist and the record company, bridging creative expression with financial needs and ensuring the project is radio-friendly and sellable. "I see a producer's role as liaison between the artist and the record company."

xref.title: "Hitler Rap" Recording Challenge
xref.body: Chris Berkett recorded Mel Brooks for "The History of the World" and "To Be or Not to Be," including the "Hitler rap." Brooks struggled to rap in time with the music, so Berkett recorded him freestyle on quarter-inch analog tape. He then had to manually mark each word with a Chinagraph pencil, pause the tape, and "drop in" each word onto a 24-track machine at the correct musical timing, a destructive and time-consuming process. "Mel Brooks couldn't rap to save his life. So the way I got the Hitler rap together was I gave up trying to get him in time with the music as impossible."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Nothing Compares 2 U" One-Take Vocal
xref.body: Sinéad O'Connor's vocal for "Nothing Compares 2 U" was a single take, followed by a perfect double track, which Chris Berkett believes would not have been captured if he had been adjusting microphones or sounds instead of being ready to record. "that was a one take vocal. If I hadn't been able to... Wait, wait, wait, wait. She sang that all the way through one take."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: AKG 414 B-ULS Microphone Use
xref.body: Steve Earle is mentioned as one of the artists who sang into Chris Berkett's preferred AKG 414 B-ULS microphone. "I've used it on Steve Earle, Chanel, O'Connor, Buffy St. Marie, Alison Moyer, they've all sung in that, that mic, it sounds great."

xref.title: Chris Berkett's Work
xref.body: Chris Berkett worked with Sting. He notes that Sting, like other well-known artists, admits that songs "come through them" rather than being consciously written. xref.title: Drum Programming Challenges on "Pyromania"
xref.body: For the album "Pyromania," producer Mutt Lange insisted on the latest technology for drums. Chris Berkett spent six weeks programming all the drums on a Fairlight CMI. This pre-MIDI process required converting the drummer's demo tapes into musical score and then typing every single event into the monophonic Fairlight using a mathematical music composition language. "And I had to write all that stuff out in score. Because it had to be converted to mathematical music language."

xref.title: Early Band with Tony Visconti Deal
xref.body: Omaha Sheriff was Chris Berkett's band that signed a record deal with Tony Visconti for a couple of albums. "my band was called Omaha Sheriff and that was Tony became my mentor while I was in the studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Online Collaboration Pioneer
xref.body: For her album "Coincidence and Likely Stories," Buffy St. Marie, living in Hawaii, collaborated with Chris Berkett in London by sending MIDI files of her keyboard parts via Compuserve (a dial-in modem service before the World Wide Web). This pioneering method allowed the album to be "born on the web." "So Roger managed to get her MIDI files onto the Compuserve and I managed to work out and download them via Compuserve into my system in London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exceptional Engineering and Separation
xref.body: Chris Berkett rediscovered The Beatles' records and was amazed by their engineering, especially the separation of instruments. He noted that despite sometimes having drums on one side and vocals on the other, the sound quality is "unbelievable how good they sound." "If you listen to those records now, it's just unbelievable how good they sound, the separation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Extensive Takes for Trumpet Solo
xref.body: Chris Berkett worked with Buena Vista Social Club on their second album, recording in his studio in the South of France. He recalls taking 250 takes of a trumpet solo and then having to edit it all together, highlighting the patience required in production. "I worked with this band, Buena Vista Social Club. I did a record with them. I'd want the second album down in my studio in South of France. And we took, the trumpet player came in and we took 250 takes of this trumpet solo, you know."

xref.title: Vocal Recording at Walter Becker's Studio
xref.body: Since Buffy St. Marie did not have a 24-track machine in her home studio, Chris Berkett had to transport 15 heavy 24-track tapes in a flight case to Walter Becker's studio in Maui to record her vocals and other parts. "I had to take a flight case full of like 1524 tracks. Really heavy. Over to Walter Becker studio, Stevie Dan studio in Maui because Buffy didn't have a 24 track machine."
